(p-٣٣٣) Surah al-Fath (The Victory)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory.﴾ *Al-fath* (الفتح) is gaining mastery over a town, either by force (عَنْوَةً, *'anwatan*) or by treaty (صُلْحًا, *sulhan*), whether through fighting or without fighting, because it remains closed (مُنْغَلِقٌ) until it is conquered; once it is conquered, it has been opened (فُتِحَ). Then it was said: it refers to the conquest of Makkah. It was revealed when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from Makkah in the year of Hudaybiyyah, as a promise to him of the conquest. It was expressed in the past tense (لَفْظِ الماضِي) because, given its certainty, it is as though it has already occurred. In this there is magnificence and an indication of the high status of what is reported, namely the conquest, which is not hidden. It was also said: it refers to the conquest of Hudaybiyyah, in which there was no fierce fighting, only shooting between the two sides with arrows and stones, until the Muslims drove the polytheists back into their dwellings and they asked for peace, so it was a clear victory. Al-Zajjaj said: In the conquest of Hudaybiyyah there was a great sign for the Muslims, for its water had been drained and not a single drop remained. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rinsed his mouth and then spat it into the well, and it gushed forth with water until all the people drank. It was also said: it refers to the conquest of Khaybar. And it was said: its meaning is, "We have decided for you a clear judgment against the people of Makkah, that you and your companions shall enter it the following year to circumambulate the House," derived from *al-fataha* (الفتاحة), which means *al-hukumah* (الحكومة), judgment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 2:

﴿That Allah may forgive you﴾. It has been said: the conquest was not the cause of the forgiveness, and the implied meaning is: "Indeed We have opened for you a clear opening, so seek forgiveness, that Allah may forgive you." Similar to this is ﴿When the help of Allah comes, and the conquest﴾ [al-Nasr: 1], up to His saying: ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness﴾ [al-Nasr: 3] (p-334). It is also permissible that the conquest of Makkah, insofar as it was a struggle against the enemy, be a cause of forgiveness. It has also been said: the conquest was not meant to forgive him; rather it was for the completion of the blessing, the guidance to the straight path, and the mighty victory. But when He enumerated these blessings upon him, He connected them to what is greater than all blessings, as if it were said: "We facilitated for you the conquest of Makkah, or such-and-such, so that We may combine for you the honour of both abodes and the aims of the immediate and the deferred."

﴿What has preceded of your sin and what has followed﴾. He means all that proceeded from you, or: what preceded of the matter of Mariyah, and what followed of the wife of Zayd.

﴿And complete His favour upon you﴾, by exalting your religion and opening the lands at your hand.

﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾, that He may keep you firm upon the pleasing religion.
[Qur'an 48:3] "And Allah will support you with a mighty victory," — ʿazīzan, meaning strong, such that there will be no humiliation after it, ever.

He it is Who sent down **tranquillity** (*al-sakina*) into the hearts of the believers, that they might increase in faith along with their faith. ﴿He it is Who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers, that they might increase in faith along with their faith.﴾ "Al-sakina" is derived from "al-sukun" (stillness), like "al-bahita" from "al-buhtan" (slander). That is, God sent down stillness and calm into their hearts, because of the peace (of al-Hudaybiyya), so that they might increase in certainty upon their certainty. It was also said that "al-sakina" means patience in what God has commanded, trust in God's promise, and glorification of God's command.

﴿And to God belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth, and God is ever Knowing, Wise.﴾ ﴿That He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and remove from them their misdeeds; and that is with God a great triumph.﴾ ﴿And that He may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and polytheist women.﴾ That is: to God belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth, He sets some of them against others as His knowledge and wisdom require. Among His decree was that He calmed the hearts of the believers through the peace of al-Hudaybiyya, and promised them that He would grant them victory. He decreed this so that the believers would recognise God's blessing in it and give thanks for it, so He would reward them, and that He would punish the disbelievers and the hypocrites for what angered and displeased them.

﴿Those who harbour an evil opinion of God.﴾ "Waq'a al-saw'" is an expression for the badness and corruption of a thing. One says "fi'l saw'" (an evil act), meaning deserving of disapproval and corrupt. What is meant is their supposition that God (Exalted) would not help the Messenger and the believers, nor would He return them to Mecca victorious, conquering it by force and compulsion. ﴿Upon them is a circle of evil.﴾ "Makki and Abu 'Amr" (read it as) "'alayhim da'iratu al-su'" (with the first "su'" pronounced with a damma): that is, what they suppose and what they wait for against the believers will encircle them and turn back upon them. "Al-su'" means destruction and ruin. Others read "da'iratu al-saw'" with a fatha: that is, the circle that they blame and detest. "Al-su'" and "al-saw'" are like "al-kurh" and "al-kurh", and "al-dha'f" and "al-du'f", except that the form with the fatha has become the usual one for what is attached to it of anything that is to be condemned. As for "al-su'", it functions in the manner of "al-sharr" (evil), which is the opposite of "al-khayr" (good).

﴿And God is angry with them, and has cursed them, and has prepared for them Hell, and evil is the destination.﴾ Jahannam.

And to Allah belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth. So He repels the plotting of whoever opposes His Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, by whatever of them He wills.

﴿And Allah is ever Exalted in Might﴾, Victorious, so His punishment cannot be turned back.

﴿All-Wise﴾ [al-Fath 48:4], in what He ordains.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 8:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾, bearing witness over your community on the Day of Resurrection. This is a *hal muqaddara* (a circumstantial qualifier referring to a future state),

﴿and a bringer of good tidings﴾, to the believers of Paradise,

﴿and a warner﴾, to the disbelievers of the Fire.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 9:

﴿That you may believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to his community.

﴿And support him﴾, that is, strengthen him with victory.

﴿And honour him﴾, that is, magnify him.

﴿And glorify Him﴾, from "al-tasbih" (glorification) or from "al-subhah" (the rosary). The pronouns refer to Allah, Exalted and Majestic. The meaning of supporting Allah is supporting His religion and His Messenger. As for one who separates the pronouns, making the first two refer to the Prophet (ﷺ), he has strayed far. ﴿That they may believe﴾ is read by Makki and Abu 'Amr, with the pronoun referring to the people; and likewise the last three are read with the "ya" (yu'minu, yusabbihu, etc.) according to these two.

﴿Morning and evening﴾: ﴿morning﴾ refers to the Fajr prayer.

﴿And evening﴾ refers to the four prayers.

﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you﴾, i.e., the pledge of ar-Ridwan (the Pledge of Ridwan). When He said ﴿Indeed, they are pledging allegiance only to Allah﴾, He emphasized this by way of *takhyil* (imaginative representation, a figurative depiction), so He said ﴿The hand of Allah is over their hands﴾. He means that the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which rises above the hands of those pledging allegiance, is the hand of Allah. Allah is exalted above bodily limbs (*jawarih*) and above the attributes of bodies. The meaning is rather to establish that the binding of the covenant with the Messenger is like its binding with Allah, without any difference between them, as in His saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [an-Nisa': 80]. And "they are pledging allegiance only to Allah" is the predicate (*khabar*) of "indeed" (*inna*).

﴿So whoever breaks [his pledge]﴾: he breaks the covenant and does not fulfill the pledge.

﴿then he breaks it only to his own detriment﴾: the harm of his breaking returns to none but himself.

Jabir ibn 'Abdullah said: "We pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) under the tree, to death, and not to flee. None of us broke the pledge except Jadd ibn Qays, who was a hypocrite. He hid beneath the belly of his camel and did not march with the people."

﴿And whoever fulfills what he has covenanted to Allah﴾: it is said "wafaytu bil-'ahd" (I fulfilled the covenant) and "awfaytu bihi" (I fulfilled it). From this is His saying: ﴿Fulfill the contracts﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1] and ﴿Those who fulfill their covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177]. ﴿عَلَيْهُ اللهَ﴾ is read by Hafs as "'alayhu Allah" (with the *damma* on the *ha*).

﴿He will give him a great reward﴾ is read with the nun (*fa-sanu'tihi*) by the Hijazi and Shami readers.

﴿A great reward﴾: Paradise.

﴿They will say to you﴾, when you return from al-Hudaybiyah, ﴿those who stayed behind of the Bedouins﴾. They are those who were left behind from al-Hudaybiyah. They were the Bedouins of Ghifar, Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Aslam, Ashja', and al-Dil. This was because when the Prophet (ﷺ) intended to set out for Makkah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah for the lesser pilgrimage (*'umrah*, a visit to the Sacred House performed outside the Hajj season), he called upon the Bedouins and the people of the desert around Madinah to go out with him. He feared that Quraysh would confront him with war or prevent him from the House. The Prophet (ﷺ) entered the state of ihram and drove the sacrificial animals (*hady*) with him, so that it would be known that he did not intend war. Many of the Bedouins held back and said: "He goes to a people who attacked him in the heart of his own home in Madinah and killed his companions, so he will fight them, and they assumed that he would be destroyed and would not return to Madinah."

﴿Our property and our families have occupied us﴾: the word *ahl* (family) is the plural here. They used as an excuse their preoccupation with their families and their property, and that there was no one to attend to their affairs.

﴿So ask forgiveness for us﴾: that Allah may forgive us our staying behind from you.

﴿They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts﴾: this is a denial of them in their excuse, and that what kept them back was not what they claimed. Rather, it was doubt concerning Allah and hypocrisy. (p-337) Their request for forgiveness is likewise not issuing from a true reality.

﴿Say: Who then controls anything for you against Allah﴾: who then can prevent you from the will and decree of Allah?

﴿If He intends harm for you﴾: what harms you, such as killing or defeat. The reading of "*ḍurran*" (harm) by Hamzah and Ali is with a damma-less form as transmitted for them.

﴿Or intends benefit for you﴾: such as spoils of war and victory.

﴿Rather, Allah is ever Aware of what you do.﴾

Verse 12 of Surah al-Fath, as quoted by al-Nasafi:

﴿Nay, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families, and that was made attractive in your hearts.﴾ [He made it attractive: Satan did.]

﴿And you thought an evil thought,﴾ [arising from the exaltation of disbelief and the spread of corruption.]

﴿And you were a people ruined.﴾ [Bur (بُورًا) is the plural of ba'ir (بائِرٌ), like ta'idh (عائِذٌ) and 'udh (عُوذٌ), from the verb bara al-shay' (بارَ الشَيْءُ), meaning it perished and became corrupt. The meaning is: you were a people corrupt in your selves, your hearts and your intentions, with no good in you; or, you were doomed in the sight of God, deserving of His wrath and His punishment.]

﴿And whoever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger – indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers a blaze.﴾ That is: for them. The explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun (al-zahir maqam al-damir, "the explicit noun in place of the pronoun"), to signal that whoever does not combine the two beliefs, belief in Allah and belief in His Messenger, is a disbeliever. He made ﴿blaze﴾ indefinite because it is a particular fire, just as he made ﴿a fire flaming﴾ [al-Layl: 14] indefinite.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 14:

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth.﴾ He manages it with the management of One who is All-Powerful and All-Wise,

﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.﴾ He forgives and He punishes by His will and His wisdom, and His wisdom is forgiveness for the believers and punishment for the disbelievers,

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ His mercy has preceded His wrath.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 15:

﴿Those who lagged behind will say﴾, namely those who stayed behind from al-Hudaybiyah,

﴿when you set out to take spoils [maghanim]﴾, that is, the spoils of Khaybar,

﴿to take them: "Let us follow you." They want to change the word of Allah﴾, "kalima Allah" (the word of Allah), read by Hamzah and ʿAli, meaning: they want to alter the promise of Allah to the people of al-Hudaybiyah. (p-338) That is because He had promised them that He would compensate them with the spoils of Khaybar when they returned, having made a truce, without having gained anything from them.

﴿Say: "You will never follow us"﴾, to Khaybar. This is a report from Allah that they will not follow them,

﴿and the word of Allah is not changed by Him.﴾

﴿Thus Allah has said before﴾, regarding their turning back to Medina, that the spoils of Khaybar belong only to those who witnessed al-Hudaybiyah, to the exclusion of others.

﴿They will say: "Rather, you envy us."﴾ That is, Allah did not command you to say this; rather, you envy us for sharing in the spoils with you.

﴿Rather, they did not understand﴾, of the word of Allah,

﴿except a little﴾, that is, except a little, meaning merely the utterance itself. The difference between the two "rather" clauses is that the first rejects that it is Allah's ruling that they should not follow them, and affirms envy; the second turns away from describing them by attributing envy to the believers, to describing them with something more grievous than that, namely ignorance and scarcity of understanding.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 16:

﴿Say to the desert Arabs who stayed behind:﴾ They are those who stayed behind from al-Hudaybiyya.

﴿You will be called to a people of great military might⁠—﴾ meaning Banu Hanifa, the people of Musaylima, and the apostates (ahl al-Ridda) whom Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) fought, because the idolatrous Arabs and the apostates are those from whom nothing is accepted except Islam or the sword. It is also said: they are Persia (Faris), and ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) did call them.

﴿You will fight them, or they will submit.﴾ That is, one of the two matters will occur: either fighting or Islam. The meaning of "yuslimun" (they submit), according to this interpretation (ta'wil), is "they yield" (yankadun), because Persia are Majus (Magians), from whom the jizya (poll tax) is accepted. The verse also indicates the soundness of the view that differs from the two Shaykhs (al-Shaykhayn, i.e., Abu Bakr and ʿUmar's position as opposed to the opposing view), in that it promises them reward for obeying the caller when he calls them, by His saying ﴿But if you obey﴾ [to fight] whoever calls you to fight him,

﴿Allah will give you a good reward,﴾ so it is necessary that the caller be one whose obedience is obligatory.

﴿But if you turn away as you turned away before⁠—﴾ that is, from al-Hudaybiyya,

﴿He will punish you with a painful punishment,﴾ in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 17:

﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick.﴾ He negated blame from those with physical infirmities regarding staying behind from the military campaign (ghazw).

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾, in jihad and other than that,

﴿He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever turns away﴾, i.e., turns away from obedience,

﴿He will punish him with a painful punishment.﴾ "Nudkhilhu" (We will admit him) and "nuʿadhdhibhu" (We will punish him) are read by the people of Medina and Syria (Madani and Shami readers) with the plural "nun" form.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾. This is the Pledge of Ridwan (bay'at al-Ridwan), so named after this verse. Its story is that "when the Prophet ﷺ alighted at al-Hudaybiyah, he sent Hirash ibn Umayyah al-Khuza'i as a messenger to Makkah. They intended to harm him, but the Ahabish (a confederation of tribes allied with Quraysh) prevented them. When he returned, he summoned Umar to send him, but he said: 'I fear for my own safety from them, because of what is known of my enmity towards them.' So he sent Uthman ibn Affan, who informed them that he had not come for war, but had come only to visit the House. They honored him and detained him with them. It was rumored that they had killed him. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'We will not depart until we fight these people,' and he called the people to the pledge. They pledged allegiance to him that they would fight Quraysh and would not flee, under the tree." It was a samurah tree (a kind of acacia), and the number of those who pledged allegiance was one thousand and four hundred.

﴿So He knew what was in their hearts﴾: of sincerity and the truthfulness of their inner intentions in what they pledged to.

﴿So He sent down tranquility upon them﴾, i.e., calm and security upon their hearts, because of the truce (sulh).

﴿And rewarded them﴾, and recompensed them,

﴿with a near victory﴾, which is the conquest of Khaybar, after their return from Makkah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 19:

﴿And much booty that they will take﴾: it refers to the spoils of Khaybar, which was land with real estate (ʿaqar) and wealth, and he (the Prophet ﷺ) distributed it among them.

﴿And Allah is ever Mighty﴾: unassailable (manīʿan), so He is not overcome;

﴿Wise﴾: in what He decrees, so He is not opposed.

God promised you many spoils that you will take. These are what they obtained with the Prophet ﷺ and after him, until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿So He hastened this for you﴾, namely the spoils, meaning the spoils of Khaybar.

﴿And restrained the hands of the people from you﴾, meaning the hands of the people of Khaybar and their allies from the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan, when they came to support them. Allah cast terror into their hearts, so they withdrew. It is also said: the hands of the people of Makkah, through the peace treaty.

﴿And that it may be a sign for the believers﴾, and a lesson, by which they recognize that they have a station with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He guarantees their victory and their triumph over their enemies, and He has done so.

﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾, and increase you in insight, certainty, and trust in the grace of Allah.

﴿And another [gain]﴾, conjoined to "هَذِهِ" (this), meaning: He hastened for you this [booty] and other booty, which is the booty of Hawazin at the Battle of Hunayn,

﴿that you were not able to obtain﴾, because of the rout that occurred in it,

﴿God has encompassed it﴾, meaning He had power over it, took possession of it, and made you prevail over it. "أُخْرى" may also be in the accusative (naṣb, the object case) governed by an implied verb (fi'l mudmar), which is explained by "قَدْ أحاطَ اللهُ بِها", its estimated form being: "وَقَضى اللهُ أُخْرى قَدْ أحاطَ بِها". As for "لَمْ تَقْدِرُوا عَلَيْها", it is a qualifier (ṣifah) of "أُخْرى", and the nominative (raf', the subject case) is by way of the inceptive (mubtada', the grammatical subject), since it is described by "لَمْ تَقْدِرُوا", and "قَدْ أحاطَ اللهُ بِها" is the predicate (khabar) of the inceptive.

﴿And God is ever Capable of everything﴾, able.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 22:

﴿And if those who disbelieve fought against you﴾, [namely] from the people of Makkah, and did not make peace, or [were] from the allies of the people of Khaybar,

﴿they would surely turn their backs﴾, they would be defeated and put to flight,

﴿then they would not find a protector﴾, one who would take charge of their affair,

﴿nor a helper﴾, one who would give them victory.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 23:

﴿Sunnata Allah (God's way)﴾ is in the position of the emphatic verbal noun (al-masdar al-mu'akkid), meaning "Allah has established the victory of His prophets as a established way (sunnatan)," which is His saying: ﴿Surely I shall prevail, I and My messengers﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21]. ﴿Which has passed before, and you will never find any change in the way of Allah﴾, meaning, any alteration.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 24:**

﴿And it is He who restrained their hands from you﴾, i.e., the hands of the people of Makkah,

﴿and your hands from them﴾, from the people of Makkah. That is, He settled between them and you the restraint (*al-mukaffah*) and the holding back (*al-muhajazah*), after He had granted you victory over them and dominance, and that was on the Day of the Conquest (*yawm al-fath*). Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, cited this verse as evidence that Makkah was conquered by force (*ʿanwatan*), not by treaty (*sulhan*). It was also said that this occurred during the Expedition of al-Hudaybiyah, based on what is narrated: "that ʿIkrimah ibn Abi Jahl set out with five hundred men, so the Messenger of God ﷺ sent someone who defeated him and drove him into the walls of Makkah." And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both: "He made the Muslims prevail over them with stones, until they drove them into their houses."

﴿in the valley of Makkah﴾, i.e., in Makkah, or at al-Hudaybiyah, because part of it is attributed to the Sacred Precinct (*al-Haram*).

﴿after He had given you victory over them﴾, i.e., He empowered you and gave you authority over them.

﴿And God is ever Seeing of what you do﴾. It is read with the yāʾ (*bi-l-yāʾ*) by Abu ʿAmr, i.e., "ya malaʾ" (*yaʿmalūna*, "they do") instead of the second-person "ta" (*taʿmalūna*, "you do").

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 48, verse 25:

﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and [barred] the sacrifice from reaching its place of sacrifice.﴾ [The word] al-hady (the sacrificial animal) refers to what is brought as an offering to the Ka'bah. It is in the accusative (naṣb) as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "kum" in "ṣaddūkum," meaning: "and they barred the sacrifice."

﴿Detained from reaching [its] place﴾, held back from reaching [its destination]. "Maʿkūfan" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). The Prophet (ﷺ) had brought seventy camels (badanah).

﴿its place of sacrifice﴾, the place where its slaughter is permitted, i.e., where it must be slaughtered. This is evidence that the place of sacrifice for one who is prevented (muḥṣar) is the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram), and the intended place is the known place of sacrifice, which is Minā.

﴿And had it not been for believing men and believing women﴾, in Makkah,

﴿whom you did not know﴾, is a description (ṣifah) of both the men and the women together,

﴿that you might trample them﴾, is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from them, or from the pronoun in the accusative in "lam taʿlamūhum,"

﴿and there would have befallen you from them a burden (maʿarrah)﴾, sin and hardship. The word "maʿarrah" is of the form "mafʿalah," from "ʿarrahu," meaning "ʿarāhu," when something he dislikes and finds burdensome befalls him. It refers to the expiation (kaffārah) if one kills him by mistake, and to the evil talk of the polytheists that they treated the people of their own religion just as they treated us, without distinction. And "al-ithm" (sin) is when it is shortened.

﴿without knowledge﴾, is connected to "an taṭa'ūhum" (that you might trample them), meaning: "that you might trample them while not knowing them." The "waṭʾ" (trampling) is an expression for inflicting and destruction. The meaning is that there were in Makkah a group of Muslims mixed with the polytheists, not distinguished from them. So it was said: "And had it not been," out of aversion to your destroying believing people amid the polytheists while you do not recognize them, so that a calamity and hardship would befall you through their destruction, once He restrained your hands from them. His saying: ﴿That Allah may admit to His mercy whom He wills﴾ is a justification for what the verse indicates and for which it was brought: the restraint of hands from the people of Makkah and the prevention of killing them, in protection of the believers who were among them. It is as if He said: "The restraint and the prevention of punishment were so that Allah might admit to His mercy — that is, to His guidance, for increase in good and obedience — their believers," or so that He might admit into Islam whoever among their polytheists desires it.

﴿Had they been separated﴾, had they been divided, and the Muslims been distinguished from the disbelievers. The answer (jawāb) to "lawlā" is omitted, and the answer of "law" has taken its place. It is permissible that "law tazayyalū" serves as a repetition for "lawlā rijālun mu'minūn," since both return to one meaning, and ﴿We would have punished those who disbelieved among them﴾ is the answer. Its estimate: "And had it not been that you might trample believing men and believing women, and had they been distinguished, We would have punished them with the sword,"

﴿among them﴾, from the people of Makkah,

﴿with a painful punishment﴾.

The governing element (al-'amil) in ﴿when those who disbelieved had put into their hearts** ﴾ — that is, Quraysh — is "la-'adhdhabna" (it means: "We would have punished them at that time"), or "udhkur" (remember).

﴿Into their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of the Jahiliyyah. So Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾. What is meant by the zealotry of those who disbelieved — and it is arrogance (al-anafah) — and by the tranquillity of the believers — and it is gravity and dignity (al-waqar) — is what is related: that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alighted at al-Hudaybiyah, Quraysh sent Suhayl ibn 'Amr, Huwaytib ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza and Mikraz ibn Hafs, on condition that they would present to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he return in that year, on condition that Quraysh would vacate Makkah for him for three days in the following year. He did so, and they wrote a document between them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "Write: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." Suhayl and his companions said: "We do not recognise this. Rather, write: 'In Your name, O Allah.'" Then he said: "Write: This is what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has agreed upon with the people of Makkah." They said: "If we knew that you are the Messenger of Allah, we would not have barred you from the House, nor fought you. Rather, write: 'This is what Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah has agreed upon with the people of Makkah.'" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Write what they want. I bear witness that I am the Messenger of Allah, and I am Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah." The Muslims were inclined to refuse that and to be repelled by it, so Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger, and they became composed and forbearing.

﴿And He made them hold fast to the word of piety﴾. The majority hold that it is the word of testimony (al-shahadah), and it has been said: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." The attribution to piety (al-taqwa) is in terms of it being the cause of piety and its foundation. It has also been said: "the word of the people of piety."

﴿And they were﴾, that is, the believers,

﴿more entitled to it﴾, than others,

﴿and worthy of it﴾, by Allah's qualifying them for it,

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing of all things﴾, so He orders matters according to their benefits.

﴿Indeed, Allah fulfilled for His Messenger the vision﴾, i.e., He made His Messenger's dream come true and did not make him a liar. (Exalted is Allah above lying.) The preposition has been omitted and the verb connected directly to its object, as in His saying: ﴿They were true to what they covenanted with Allah concerning it﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23]. It was narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw, before he set out for al-Hudaybiyya, that he and his Companions had entered Makkah in safety, with some of them having shaved their heads and some having trimmed their hair. He related the vision to his Companions, and they rejoiced and thought they would enter it that same year. They said, "The vision of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is true." When that was delayed, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and others said, "By Allah, we did not shave our heads, nor trim our hair, and we did not see the Sacred Mosque." Then it was revealed:

﴿with the truth﴾ is connected to *ṣadaqa* (fulfilled), i.e., "He fulfilled it in what he saw, and in its occurrence and realization as a truth mixed with the truth," that is, with consummate wisdom (*al-ḥikmah al-bāligah*), and that includes the trial and the distinguishing between the sincere believer and the one in whose heart is a sickness. It is also permissible that *bi-l-ḥaqq* be an oath: either *bi-l-ḥaqq* meaning the opposite of falsehood, or *bi-l-ḥaqq* being one of His names. Its answer is ﴿you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾. According to the first, it is the answer of an omitted oath (*qasam maḥdhūf*).

﴿if Allah wills﴾ is a report from Allah, the Exalted, of the words of His Messenger to his Companions and their relating it to him; or it is an instruction to His servants that they should say the like when they make promises, following the courtesy of Allah and emulating His practice.

﴿in safety﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and the conditional clause (*al-sharṭ*) is a parenthetical insertion (*mu'tariḍ*).

﴿having shaved﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *āminīn* (in safety).

﴿your heads﴾, i.e., all of their hair.

﴿and trimming﴾, some of their hair.

﴿you do not fear﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial clause (*ḥāl mu'akkidah*).

﴿So He knew what you did not know﴾, of the wisdom in delaying the conquest of Makkah until the following year. (p-344) ﴿Then He made, besides that,﴾ i.e., besides the conquest of Makkah,

﴿a near victory﴾, which is the conquest of Khaybar, so that the hearts of the believers might find rest in it until the promised conquest became possible.

He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance, [that is,] with monotheism (tawhid),

and the religion of truth, i.e., Islam,

to make it prevail, to exalt it, over all religion, over the genus of religion, meaning the various religions, among them the religions of the polytheists and the People of the Book. And indeed He, glory be to Him, has fulfilled this; for you do not see any religion at all except that Islam has, beyond it, might and dominance. It has been said: it refers to the time of the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him, when no disbeliever will remain on the face of the earth. It has also been said: it means prevailing through proofs and signs.

And sufficient is Allah as a witness, [as a witness] that what He promised is certain to happen. It is related from al-Hasan: "He bore witness for Himself that He would make His religion prevail." The implied meaning is: "And Allah suffices him as a witness." And "witness" (shahidan) is a specification (tamyiz) or a circumstantial accusative (hal).

﴿Muhammad﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an inchoative subject (mubtada', the topic of a nominal sentence), meaning "He is Muhammad," because of the preceding statement ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger﴾. Alternatively, it is the mubtada', and its predicate is ﴿the Messenger of Allah﴾, on which Nusayr stopped (waqf).

﴿Those who are with him﴾, meaning his companions, is a mubtada', and its predicate is ﴿severe against the disbelievers﴾. Or, "Muhammad" is the mubtada', "the Messenger of Allah" is an explicative apposition ('atf bayan), "those who are with him" is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the mubtada', and "severe" (ashidda'') is a predicate for all of them. Its meaning is: harsh (ghilaz).

﴿Merciful among themselves﴾: they show compassion to one another. This is a second predicate. The two words are the plural forms of "shadid" (severe) and "rahim" (merciful). A similar expression is ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty toward the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54]. Their severity toward the disbelievers went so far that they would guard their garments from touching the garments of the disbelievers, and their bodies from touching their bodies. Their mercy toward one another went so far that whenever a believer saw another believer, he would shake his hand and embrace him.

﴿You see them bowing (ruka'an)﴾, meaning bowing in prostration (raki'in).

﴿Prostrating (sujjadan)﴾, meaning prostrating (sajidin).

﴿Seeking﴾ (yabtaghun) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), just as "ruka'an" and "sujjadan" are circumstantial accusatives.

﴿Bounty from Allah and approval. Their mark﴾ (simahum) means their sign.

﴿In their faces is the trace of prostration﴾, meaning the effect that prostration leaves. It is related from 'Ata': "Their faces shone from how long they prayed (p-٣٤٥) at night," in accordance with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever prays much at night, his face will be beautiful by day."

﴿That﴾, meaning what has been mentioned, is ﴿their likeness﴾ (mathaluhum), meaning their description.

﴿In the Torah﴾: a pause (waqf) is made here.

﴿And their likeness in the Gospel﴾ is a mubtada', whose predicate is ﴿like a seed that sends out its shoot﴾ (shat'ahu), meaning its offshoots. It is said: "the crop sent out shoots" (ashta'a al-zar'u) when it put forth sprouts.

﴿Then strengthens it﴾ (fa-azarahu) means it strengthened it. "Fa'azarahu" is the reading of the Syrian reader (Shami).

﴿Then it becomes thick﴾ (fastaghlaza): it went from thinness to thickness.

﴿Then it stands firm on its stalk﴾ means it stood straight on its stem; "suq" is the plural of "saq" (stalk).

﴿Pleasing the farmers﴾: they marvel at its strength. It is also said that it is written in the Gospel: "A people will come forth who sprout like the growth of the crop; they will enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil." It is related from 'Ikrimah: "It sent out its shoot with Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), it strengthened it with 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), it became thick with 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him), and it stood firm on its stalk with 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them all)." This is a parable that Allah (Exalted) set forth for the beginning of Islam and its progress in growth until it became strong and firmly established, because the Prophet (ﷺ) stood alone at first, then Allah (Exalted) strengthened him with those who believed with him, just as the first shoot of the crop is surrounded by what grows out of it, until it pleases the farmers.

﴿That He may enrage the disbelievers by them﴾ is a statement of cause (ta'lil) for what their likeness to the crop indicates of their growth, their progress in increase and strength. It is also permissible that the cause be ﴿Allah has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward﴾, because when the disbelievers hear of what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter, along with the honor they are given in this world, it enrages them. The "min" in ﴿from among them﴾ is explicative (lil-bayan), as in His saying: ﴿So avoid the filth of idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], meaning: avoid the filth which is idols; and as in your saying: "Spend from the dirhams," meaning: make your expenditure of this kind. This verse refutes the claim of the Rawafid (a term for a group of Shi'a) that they disbelieved after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), since the promise to them of forgiveness and a great reward applies only if they remained steadfast in what they were upon during his lifetime.
